# Abstract

Recent advancements in Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) show promise for pathological diagnosis, yet their application in clinical settings faces critical challenges of multimodal hallucination and biased responses. While preference alignment methods have proven effective in general domains, acquiring high-quality preference data for pathology remains challenging due to limited expert resources and domain complexity. In this paper, we propose EAGLE (Expert-guided self-enhancement for preference Alignment in patholoGy Large vision-language model), a novel framework that systematically integrates medical expertise into preference alignment. EAGLE consists of three key stages: initialization through supervised fine-tuning, self-preference creation leveraging expert prompting and medical entity recognition, and iterative preference following-tuning. The self-preference creation stage uniquely combines expert-verified chosen sampling with expert-guided rejected sampling to generate high-quality preference data, while the iterative tuning process continuously refines both data quality and model performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EAGLE significantly outperforms existing pathological LVLMs, effectively reducing hallucination and bias while maintaining pathological accuracy. The source code is available at https://github.com/meidandz/EAGLE.

# 2 Related Work

# 2.1 Medical Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs)

Recent LLM advancements have transformed vision-language models (Li et al., 2024a; Yin et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024), with models like LLaVA (Liu et al., 2024b) achieving GPT-4-level performance. In medicine, LLaVA-Med (Li et al., 2024b) and BiomedGPT (Zhang et al., 2024) pioneered innovations, with BiomedGPT training on 271,803 image-text pairs. While MedDr (He et al., 2024) and STLLaVA-Med (Sun et al., 2024) advanced healthcare applications, histopathology remained underserved. PathChat (Lu et al., 2023), adapted from LLaVA and fine-tuned on 450k instruction pairs, later outperformed GPT-4V in

pathology tasks. Quilt-LLaVA (Seyfioglu et al., 2024), trained on the Quilt-instruct dataset and Quilt-VQA's 107,131 QA pairs, further advanced pathology capabilities. Meanwhile, Xie et al. proposed the MedTrinity-25M dataset and used this dataset to pretrain LLaVA, surpassing representative SOTA multimodal large language models. However, challenges like high construction costs and alignment issues persist. Thus, we propose a self-creation stage to synthesize preference data automatically.

# 2.2 Preference Learning in LVLM

Preference learning is essential for developing effective (Gorbatovski et al., 2024), safe (Dai et al., 2023), and trustworthy (Yu et al., 2024) models. It typically follows an instruction-following stage, where models are fine-tuned using human input. Cui et al. propose a data-centric framework, Biomedical Visual Instruction Tuning with Clinician Preference Alignment (BioMed-VITAL), that incorporates clinician preferences into both stages of generating and selecting instruction data for tuning biomedical multimodal foundation models. Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) (Ouyang et al., 2022) is a widely used method, involving a reward model trained on human preferences to guide policy optimization. Since RLHF is complex and unstable, requiring reward model training and fine-tuning of large unsupervised models to maximize rewards, several RLHF variants have been developed, including Direct Policy Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2024), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017), and Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) (Bai et al., 2022). DPO simplifies the process by bypassing the reward model and directly learning policies, reducing complexity and often outperforming PPO. Zhu et al. propose MMedPO, a novel multimodal medical preference optimization approach that considers the clinical relevance of preference samples to enhance Med-LVLM alignment. In this work, we propose EAGLE to iteratively align specially for pathology LVLMs with preference data optimized by DPO.

\mathcal {D} = \left\{\mathbf {Q} _ {i}, \mathbf {A} _ {i} ^ {c}, \mathbf {A} _ {i} ^ {r} \right\} _ {i = 1} ^ {N}, \tag {1}
$$

where $\mathbf{A}_i^c$ is generated through expert-verified chosen sampling and $\mathbf{A}_i^r$ through expert-guided rejected sampling.

Expert-Guided Rejected Sampling (EGRS). In Fig. 4, we propose an expert-guided rejected sampling module to utilize multiple experts to analyze the pathological findings of the input image and further generate rejected responses based on the findings.

Concretely, given an input image $\mathbf{X}_i$ , we extract patches for $\mathbf{X}_i$ and establish a pathology expert panel to screen the abnormality of each patch $\mathbf{X}_i^j$ , where $j$ indicates the $j$ -th patch of the input image. The pathology expert panel consists of four pathological expert models, including UNI (Chen et al., 2024), CTransPath (Wang et al., 2022), Enhanced ViT (Ding et al., 2023), and Phikon (Filiot et al., 2023). Each expert model provides the decision on the presence of tumors for each patch. To provide overall pathological findings, we perform a majority vote on the decisions from all the expert models. Then, we generate the rejected response based on the presence of the tumor. When the input image contains tumor regions, we generate a mask image $\mathcal{M}$ that indicates the tumor patches, and perform element-wise multiplication between $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathbf{X}_i$ to generate a masked input image ( $\mathcal{M} \odot \mathbf{X}_i$ ). $$

where prompt $\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{r}}$ is designed to guide the model in generating responses that maintain pathological relevance while introducing controlled semantic deviations. Please see Appendix D for details.

For images without tumor regions, we first apply a Medical Named Entity Recognition (NER) model (Mattupalli, 2025) to identify pathological entities in both the chosen response and the ground-truth (GT) answer. We then perform exact matching between the entities of the chosen response $\mathbf{E}^c$ and GT answer $\mathbf{E}^{gt}$ to identify matched and unmatched entities: $\mathbf{E}^c = \{\mathbf{E}_m^c,\mathbf{E}_u^c\}$ , $\mathbf{E}^{gt} = \left\{\mathbf{E}_m^{gt},\mathbf{E}_u^{gt}\right\}$ , where $m$ and $u$ denote 'matched' and 'unmatched', respectively. To generate the rejected response, we replace matched entities $\mathbf{E}_m^c$ from the chosen response with unmatched entities $\mathbf{E}_u^{gt}$ from the GT answer, creating a synthetic response that introduces controlled inaccuracies while maintaining pathological coherence. These perturbations are carefully designed to reflect realistic diagnostic errors, ensuring that the rejected samples maintain a high degree of relevance to real-world scenarios. Finally, we refine this synthetic response through LVLM-SFT to improve its coherence, yielding the final rejected response. This approach ensures rejected responses contain plausible but incorrect diagnostic information, providing effective training signals for preference optimization.

# 3.3 Preference Following-Tuning

Aiming to align the SFT-tuned LVLM (LVLM-SFT) with the synthetic preference data, we introduce Preference Following-Tuning (PFT) to learn from the preference data iteratively. Specifically, we adopt Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2024) to implement preference alignment, which can be viewed as a new parameterization of the reward model in RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) (Ouyang et al., 2022) that can directly optimize the policy model $\pi_{\mathrm{pre}}$ . The policy model is optimized as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l} L _ {d p o} (\pi_ {p r e}; \pi_ {\theta}) = - E _ {(m, \mathbf {A} _ {i} ^ {c}, \mathbf {A} _ {i} ^ {r})} \sim \mathcal {D} \\ \left[ \log \sigma (\beta l o g \frac {\pi_ {p r e} \left(\mathbf {A} _ {i} ^ {c} \mid m\right)}{\pi_ {\theta} \left(\mathbf {A} _ {i} ^ {c} \mid m\right)} \right. \tag {4} \\ \left. - \beta \log \frac {\pi_ {p r e} (\mathbf {A} _ {i} ^ {r} | m)}{\pi_ {\theta} (\mathbf {A} _ {i} ^ {r} | m)} \right], \\ \end{array}
$$

where $m = (\mathbf{X}_i,\mathbf{Q})$ , and is the input to the LVLM $\pi_{pre}$ . $\pi_{\mathrm{pre}}$ and $\pi_{\theta}$ denote policy model and reference model, respectively. $\mathcal{D}$ represents our preference dataset, and $\log \sigma$ stands for log-sigmoid function. This objective function is designed to train the reward and policy models concurrently, skewing the reward model to favor the chosen response and reject the rejected response.

To enhance the quality of preference alignment, we implement stages 2 and 3 alternately, allowing iterative refinement of both chosen and rejected responses using the progressively improved LVLM-PFT model. This creates a positive feedback loop where preference dataset evolves alongside model improvements, leading to enhanced response quality and more effective preference alignment.

The results also demonstrate the significant contributions of EVCS in preference data creation. # 5 Conclusion In this paper, we presented EAGLE, a novel framework for enhancing pathology-focused LVLMs through expert-guided preference alignment. EAGLE addresses multimodal hallucination and biased responses through a three-stage approach that generates high-quality preference data without extensive manual expert annotation. Extensive experiments across multiple pathology datasets demonstrate EAGLE's superiority over existing LVLMs, achieving the best performance in visual question answering, visual prompting tasks, and multimodal conversations. # Limitations Although our method achieved promising experimental results, it was primarily designed for pathology applications. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), in particular, demonstrates strong robustness to noise and label inconsistencies through several key properties: Noise Samples Have Local Impact: DPO only uses pairwise preference comparisons, so a mislabeled pair affects only the loss from that specific comparison. It does not distort the absolute scores or global preference structure. The loss function for a noisy pair is given as: $$ \begin{array}{l} \mathcal {L} ^ {\text {n o i s y}} = - \log \sigma (- \beta (\log \pi_ {\theta} (y ^ {w} | x) \\ \left. - \log \pi_ {\theta} \left(y ^ {l} | x\right)\right) \Bigg) \tag {5} \\ \end{array} $$ where the flipped gradient only affects the local direction for the specific triple $(x, y^w, y^l)$ . The rest of the dataset remains unaffected. Correct Preferences Outweigh Noisy Ones: Since DPO relies on many preference pairs, noisy labels are diluted by the majority of correct comparisons. The model's update direction reflects the dominant preference signal. The update direction for the model parameters is computed as: $$ \nabla_ {\theta} \mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {D P O}} = - \beta (\sigma (\beta \Delta) - 1) \nabla_ {\theta} \Delta $$ $$ \text {w h e r e} \quad \Delta = \log \pi_ {\theta} \left(y ^ {w} | x\right) - \log \pi_ {\theta} \left(y ^ {l} | x\right) \tag {6} $$ Even if some $\Delta < 0$ due to noise, most updates push in the correct direction when $\Delta > 0$ dominates. DPO Is Inherently Robust to Label Scale Bias: Unlike reward modeling or pointwise RLHF methods, DPO does not require consistent or absolute reward values.
